INF2002 · Team 08 · Implementation notes

From paper prototype to working interactions

Clarity preserves the team’s pre-send privacy review and information dashboard. This document maps implemented decisions to the supplied evidence and explains the compromises.

Open prototypeResearcher consoleTesting guide

Materials and authority

The three team submissions describe research and design work. The Studio 6 document is the assignment brief. Lecture decks provide concepts and methods; their classroom exercises and administrative directions are not additional feature requests. The user’s latest scope and supplied instructor feedback determine this implementation.

  • Assignment 1: 50 survey responses and six numbered interview transcripts are present. The report identifies five user needs. Not all survey questions use the same denominator; the usefulness statistic specifically describes 34 responses.
  • Assignment 2: eight concepts A–H; selected combination of pre-send warnings and a dashboard, with Shared in Chats, Saved Preferences, and Possible Inferences.
  • Assignment 3: six heuristic evaluators; think-aloud findings about missed alerts, additional-information controls, dashboard discovery, and return navigation. Think-aloud participant count and participant-level outcomes are insufficiently specified; no prevalence is inferred.
  • Paper images: empty chat, alert, expanded review, explanatory card, changed prompt, dashboard, item details, and deletion confirmation.
  • Lectures reviewed: Introduction; History of HCI; User Centered Design; Needfinding; Task Analysis; Usability Principles; Evaluation; Visual Design; Ethics; Prototyping; Human Abilities; Web Interaction; Mobile Interaction.
  • Instructor feedback: explicit action names, consistent primary/secondary styling, red destructive actions, stronger typography, reuse picker, item-removed feedback, deletion scope, more complete evaluation reporting, and less participant coaching.

Research needs preserved

  1. Know which personal information is necessary for the current task.
  2. Detect and review potentially sensitive details before sending.
  3. Choose a level of privacy support appropriate to the context.
  4. Control reuse of individual details across conversations.
  5. See what was shared, intentionally saved, or possibly inferred.

The survey’s 34% review-pause and 32% non-interrupting-notice preferences support both warning modes. The reported 50% preference for choosing or approving reuse supports default rules and individual exceptions. These findings motivate design choices; they do not prove that this implementation is usable.

Screens and numbered flows

1. Chat → write initial prompt or follow-up → inspect underline or nearby warning → 2. Review card → compare original / replacement → mask, generalise, keep or manually edit → undo if needed → send → scripted response.

1. Chat → floating shield widget or menu → 3. Privacy dashboard → search/filter → 4. Information details → correct value / choose reuse rule / delete → scope confirmation → completion and Removed → restore or permanently delete.

Menu → 5. Privacy preferences → warning mode / categories / default reuse → save → test reuse example.
Menu → 6. Help → simulation limits, storage, deletion, keyboard controls.
Each participant screen has a route back to chat. Drafts belong to individual conversations and survive navigation and reload.

The frequent dashboard path also has a direct labelled control.
Squiggly underlines plus a nearby warning with countAssignment 3 pp.7–8: participants missed the standalone alert while composing.Feedback, mapping, gulfs of execution/evaluation: Usability Principles pp.34–38, 54.Greater visibility can distract while writing. The controlled comparison removes only underlines to evaluate that benefit.
Original and replacement shown together, with a short reason and optional detailAssignment 1 pp.4–6: preserve useful context and avoid long explanations; Assignment 3: more-info control missed.Recognition and split attention: Human Abilities pp.33, 39, 42. Progressive disclosure: Web Interaction p.27.The compact explanation cannot communicate every context-dependent privacy risk.
Mask information, Generalise, Keep unchanged, Edit manuallyAssignment 2 pp.4–7 and Assignment 3 pp.4–6: users need explicit choices; tick/cross meanings were ambiguous.User control, signifiers, consistency: Usability Principles pp.28, 60–63.More choices require reading. Keep is an intentional decision, not counted as a failure whenever context is useful.
Review selected replacements together; undo a batch in one stepFive heuristic evaluators raised efficiency concerns; several flagged details must be manageable.Efficiency, constraints, reversible actions: Evaluation pp.27, 32; History of HCI p.36.Batch review can encourage mechanical acceptance, so before/after values and individual checkboxes remain visible.
Notice or review-pause preferences; no automatic rewritingAssignment 1: 34% pause, 32% notice; interview desire to check changes before applying.User-centred design and user control: User Centered Design pp.7–9, 16.Notice mode permits unreviewed sends; pause mode adds friction. Neither mode claims guaranteed protection.

Help explains storage and reset.
Three provenance groups; possible inferences explicitly unconfirmedAssignment 1 need 5; Assignment 2 pp.6–7 distinguishes shared facts, saved preferences and inference.Mental models and system image: Usability Principles pp.50–54.A fixed fictional inference illustrates the concept but cannot evaluate real inference quality.
Default reuse rule plus individual item overrides and a working exampleHalf of survey respondents preferred selecting or approving reuse; instructor requested reuse-mode picker.Visibility, mapping and control: Usability Principles pp.31, 38, 60–63.Two rule levels add complexity. Delete / Cancel; scope list; Removed list and restoreAssignment 3 pp.5–8 and latest HCI review: deletion scope and recovery were unclear.Error prevention/recovery, feedback, familiar language: Evaluation pp.24, 27, 32, 47.Recoverable copies remain locally stored until permanent deletion. Confirmation explains that chat text and exports remain.
One green primary accent; amber warnings; red destructive controls; text and iconsFive evaluators reported colour inconsistency; latest feedback asks for red destructive actions and readable text.Visual hierarchy, colour/contrast, Gestalt grouping: Visual Design pp.6–12, 25, 31–35, 43, 47–49.Colour alone is insufficient; labels and patterns carry meaning. Dense researcher tables are separated from participant UI.

Automated checks are incomplete evidence.

Collect voluntary explanations separately, without leading them.

Conflicts resolved and scope limits

  • Extension versus prototype: the earlier submission describes an extension. The current user request takes precedence: this build is static HTML/CSS/JavaScript with no actual GPT or browser-extension integration.
  • Attachments: research mentions screenshots/documents, but robust attachment scanning is outside the requested primary text journey. The UI does not display a misleading upload control.
  • Yes versus action labels: some revised drawings still say Yes. The instructor’s latest feedback and current requirements favour explicit actions.
  • Menu versus dashboard shield: sketches use both. A top-left menu holds all screens; a draggable floating shield widget opens a quick menu to every screen, so it can be moved away from whatever content it covers.
  • “Safe prompt”: replaced with precise feedback such as “No matches found” because deterministic detection cannot guarantee safety.
  • Research gaps: no separate persona document or raw participant-by-task think-aloud record was provided. The implementation uses fictional scenarios; it does not fabricate personas, participant quotes, outcomes or validation claims. One transcript includes a “rehearsal example” label, which should be clarified in the report before treating it as verbatim evidence.
  • Study consent: disclose general purpose, tasks, recording and rights. Withhold only the precise comparison hypothesis during tasks; the assignment’s instruction not to reveal it does not replace informed consent.

Report improvements still requiring the team’s evidence

Move the current-workflow HTA into the main report, discuss its strengths, weaknesses and social setting, and add explicit privacy decisions before initial and follow-up sends. Describe actual recruitment, counts and procedures in past tense; include real consent documentation and warm-up/cool-down material. Name and caption storyboard panels, include a rejected alternative and justification, and show larger numbered screens and arrows. For evaluation, add actual participant-by-task quotes, outcomes and assistance rather than “most users.” The testing guide includes a blank recording template; it is not filled with invented results.

Source references use PDF page numbers, including cover pages. All cited documents were provided by the user. The prototype is an implementation to evaluate, not evidence of improved usability.
